content: A potato chip, also known as a crisp in some regions, is a thinly sliced piece of potato that is either deep-fried or baked until it becomes crispy. These chips are commonly consumed as appetizers, side dishes, or snacks. Commercially produced potato chips are typically sold in bags. The simplest form of potato chips is cooked and salted, but manufacturers often enhance their flavor by adding a variety of seasonings, which may include herbs, spices, cheese, artificial additives, or monosodium glutamate (MSG). Potato chips are a significant component of the snack food industry, particularly in English-speaking countries and other Western nations. The terminology for fried potato products varies across English-speaking regions. In North America, the term chips refers to the thin, crispy slices of potato, while French fries describes the hot, soft-centered potato batons. In the United Kingdom and Ireland, crisps are the thin, brittle slices eaten at room temperature, whereas chips refer to the hot, fried potato dish, as in fish and chips. In Australia, New Zealand, and parts of South Africa, both forms of potato products are generally called chips, with distinctions sometimes made between hot chips (French fries) and packet chips (potato chips). Non-potato-based chips also exist, such as sweet potato chips in New Zealand and Japan or parsnip crisps in the United Kingdom. Regional variations include fried sliced potatoes called flakies in parts of Northern England and a wide variety of plantain, yam, and carrot chips sold in India. Potato chips have faced criticism in many countries due to their high fat content (approximately 35%) and the presence of acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound formed during high-temperature cooking. The origin of the potato chip is often attributed to George Crum, a Native American/African American chef at Moon's Lake House near Saratoga Springs, New York, on August 24, 1853. Crum reportedly created the dish in response to a customer, possibly Cornelius Vanderbilt, who repeatedly complained that his fried potatoes were too thick and soggy. To address the complaint, Crum sliced the potatoes extremely thin, fried them until crisp, and served them. Contrary to his expectations, the customer was delighted, and the dish, named Saratoga Chips, became a staple on the restaurant's menu. The popularity of potato chips spread throughout New York and New England, eventually transitioning from a restaurant specialty to a mass-produced snack. The Mike-sell's Potato Chip Company, founded in Dayton, Ohio, in 1910, claims to be the oldest potato chip company in the United States. Historically, it takes approximately four pounds of raw potatoes to produce one pound of potato chips. Before the invention of airtight packaging, potato chips were stored in barrels or tins, which often left the chips at the bottom stale and damp. Laura Scudder revolutionized chip storage in the 1920s by creating an airtight bag using two pieces of waxed paper sealed together. This innovation kept chips fresh until opened. In 1934, K.T. Salem of Akron, Ohio, became the first to distribute chips in glassine waxed paper bags. Modern packaging involves plastic bags filled with nitrogen gas to extend shelf life and protect the chips from crushing. The global potato chip market generated $16.4 billion in revenue in 2005, accounting for 35.5% of the total savory snacks market, which was valued at $46.1 billion that year. Initially, potato chips were sold unseasoned, with a small twist of salt included in the bag for optional flavoring. This practice was introduced by the Smiths Potato Crisps Company Ltd in 1920. However, the process of seasoning chips during manufacturing was pioneered by Joe Spud Murphy, the owner of the Irish company Tayto, in the 1950s. Murphy developed a method to add seasonings directly to the chips, creating the first flavored varieties, such as Cheese and Onion and Salt 'n' Vinegar. This innovation transformed the potato chip industry, leading to widespread adoption of flavored chips and making Murphy and his family wealthy when the Tayto company was sold. Today, potato chips are available in a vast array of flavors, with regional preferences influencing the popularity of specific seasonings. In the United States, popular potato chip flavors include sour cream and onion, barbecue, and ranch. In the Chesapeake Bay area, crab chips seasoned with Old Bay-style spices are common. Canada offers a broader range of flavors, such as dill pickle, ketchup, poutine, and wasabi. In the United Kingdom, Walkers dominates the market with flavors like salt & vinegar, cheese & onion, prawn cocktail, and more exotic options like Thai sweet chili and lamb with Moroccan spices. In Japan, unique flavors include nori & salt, wasabi, soy sauce & butter, and takoyaki. Manufacturers like Calbee and Koikeya lead the Japanese market. Alternative types of chips include those made from dough formed from ground potatoes, such as Pringles, which are uniform in size and shape and packaged in rigid tubes. Baked potato chips with reduced fat content and fat-free chips made with artificial fat substitutes like Olestra have also been introduced, though the latter has been associated with gastrointestinal side effects in some individuals. The success of potato chips has inspired similar products, such as fried corn chips (e.g., Fritos and Doritos) and chips made from root vegetables like parsnips and carrots. Potato chips are also used in various recipes, including as a topping for casseroles, a breading for meats, or an ingredient in dips. In some regions, chips are incorporated into sandwiches, such as the chip butty in the UK or the Marmite and chip sandwich in New Zealand. Some individuals prefer to refrigerate or freeze chips before consumption, a practice that elicits mixed reactions.
